source_document.body:
Nearly half of the supply chain organizations in a Gartner survey reduced headcount primarily because of AI over the past two years, with those organizations reporting an average reduction of 10.5%. Entry-level employees have been especially affected as companies change how work gets done.
What’s Related
Gartner found that 47% of the supply chains surveyed had cut staff primarily due to AI. Separately, 66% of leaders reported a decline in entry-level headcount, more than double the share reporting reductions at other levels.
The findings come from organizations that already use AI in their workflows to some degree. They do not represent a survey of the entire supply chain industry.
“AI is thinning the entry-level supply chain workforce faster than most chief supply chain officers (CSCOs) are redesigning the talent pipeline, creating a future capability gap that will actually weaken their organizations’ AI performance,” said Tess Frenzel, Director Analyst in Gartner’s Supply Chain practice.
Fewer new hires, fewer future leaders
Gartner said cutting entry-level hiring without changing what those employees do could leave companies with fewer people prepared to move into senior positions. Supply chains have traditionally relied on a large pool of junior employees to develop future leaders, even when many leave along the way.
A smaller incoming group makes hiring, training, and retaining promising employees more important. At the same time, Gartner found that expectations for middle-management skills have changed compared with two years ago.
“Producing fewer candidates for traditionally defined leadership roles is a miscalculation, as supply chains will require new competencies both for entry-level and leadership positions as a result of working alongside AI,” Frenzel said.
RELATED STORIES: Eight Ways AI is Transforming the Modern Warehouse | Six Supply Chain AI Developments Worth Watching
Changing the entry-level job
Gartner’s analysis found that its highest-performing supply chains are raising expectations for entry-level employees. The firm defined that group as the top 25% based on AI integration, AI-enabled automation , and business outcomes.
“Compared with two years ago, these organizations require more domain-specific and analytics skills and greater supply chain experience, while involving entry-level employees in less repetitive work and more consequential decisions,” Frenzel said.
Gartner recommends three steps to help supply chain leaders prepare junior employees for more demanding roles:
Pair junior employees with experienced colleagues. Match technically skilled entry-level employees with mid- and senior-level staff to build business knowledge while helping deploy and oversee AI.
Make responsibility for AI clear. Track AI usage, regularly test the data and assumptions behind its models, and assign clear accountability for results.
Build teams across supply chain functions. Bring employees from different areas together to share knowledge and work toward common performance goals.
